question: When two power-driven vessels are approaching each other head-on, what should each operator do?
choice_a: The larger vessel should always reverse
choice_b: Each should alter course to starboard (right) so the vessels pass port-to-port, like cars on a two-lane road
choice_c: Both should alter course to port so the vessels pass starboard-to-starboard
choice_d: Neither vessel should change course under any circumstance
explanation: In a head-on meeting, the Navigation Rules direct each power-driven vessel to alter course to starboard, resulting in a safe port-to-port passing, similar to the convention for cars meeting on a road.
source_note: Universal Navigation Rules (Inland Rule 14), NASBLA-aligned boating safety curriculum

question: In a crossing situation between two power-driven vessels, which vessel is the "stand-on" vessel that should maintain its course and speed?
choice_a: The vessel that sounds its horn first always has the right-of-way
choice_b: Both vessels must always come to a complete stop
choice_c: The vessel that has the other vessel approaching on its own port (left) side is the stand-on vessel; the vessel with the other boat on its starboard side must give way
choice_d: Whichever vessel is moving faster automatically has the right-of-way
explanation: In a crossing situation, the vessel that sees the other vessel on its own starboard side is the give-way vessel and must take early, substantial action to avoid a collision, while the other vessel is the stand-on vessel.
source_note: Universal Navigation Rules (Inland Rule 15), NASBLA-aligned boating safety curriculum

question: When one vessel is overtaking another, which vessel must give way?
choice_a: The vessel being overtaken must always speed up to stay ahead
choice_b: The overtaking vessel automatically becomes the stand-on vessel
choice_c: Right-of-way in overtaking situations is decided by vessel size alone
choice_d: The overtaking vessel must keep clear of the vessel being overtaken, regardless of whether the overtaking vessel is a sailboat or powerboat
explanation: The overtaking vessel is always the give-way vessel and must keep clear of the vessel it is passing until it is safely past and clear, no matter what type either vessel is.
source_note: Universal Navigation Rules (Inland Rule 13), NASBLA-aligned boating safety curriculum

question: Between a sailing vessel under sail alone and a power-driven vessel, which generally has right-of-way?
choice_a: The sailing vessel generally has right-of-way over the power-driven vessel
choice_b: The power-driven vessel always has right-of-way
choice_c: Right-of-way is determined solely by which vessel is larger
choice_d: Sailing vessels have no right-of-way status under the Navigation Rules
explanation: A sailing vessel operating under sail alone generally has right-of-way over a power-driven vessel, though a sailboat also uses its engine, it is legally a power-driven vessel and loses that special status.
source_note: Universal Navigation Rules (Inland Rule 18), NASBLA-aligned boating safety curriculum

question: What one prolonged blast of a horn generally means when leaving a dock or blind bend on Nevada waters?
choice_a: A signal used only by law enforcement vessels
choice_b: A warning signal alerting other vessels that a boat is approaching a blind area, such as leaving a slip or rounding a point where visibility is limited
choice_c: A request for another vessel to stop completely
choice_d: An announcement that the vessel is about to anchor
explanation: One prolonged blast is the warning signal used when a vessel is approaching a bend or an area where other traffic may not be visible, alerting nearby boaters of its presence.
source_note: Universal Navigation Rules sound signal conventions (Inland Rule 34), NASBLA-aligned boating safety curriculum

question: What does one short blast of a horn mean when signaling another power-driven vessel during a meeting or crossing situation?
choice_c: "I intend to leave you on my port side" (I am altering course to starboard)
explanation: One short blast signals an intent to alter course to starboard, meaning the signaling vessel will leave the other vessel on its port side; two short blasts signal an intent to leave the other vessel on the starboard side.
source_note: Universal Navigation Rules sound signals (Inland Rule 34), NASBLA-aligned boating safety curriculum

question: On a narrow stretch of the Colorado River between Lake Mead and Lake Mohave, which vessels generally must not impede the passage of the other?
choice_a: In narrow channels, small vessels always have unconditional right-of-way over larger ones
choice_b: There are no special rules for narrow channels
choice_c: Sailing vessels always have unconditional priority in narrow channels
choice_d: A vessel that can safely navigate only within a narrow channel has a special status, and other vessels, including sailing vessels and vessels under 20 meters, must not impede its safe passage in that channel
explanation: The Navigation Rules' narrow-channel provision gives priority to a vessel that can only navigate safely within the channel, requiring other vessels not to impede its passage, a rule especially relevant on constrained river stretches like the Colorado River below Hoover Dam.
source_note: Universal Navigation Rules (Inland Rule 9) applied to the Colorado River corridor between Lake Mead and Lake Mohave

question: What action should the give-way vessel take under the Navigation Rules?
choice_a: Take early and substantial action to keep well clear of the other vessel, avoiding a series of small course changes
choice_b: Wait until the last possible moment to react
choice_c: Speed up to cross ahead of the stand-on vessel as quickly as possible
choice_d: Turn off all navigation lights to avoid detection
explanation: The give-way vessel is required to act early and decisively, making a course or speed change large enough to be obvious to the other vessel, rather than a series of small, ambiguous adjustments.
source_note: Universal Navigation Rules (Inland Rule 16), NASBLA-aligned boating safety curriculum

question: What should the stand-on vessel do if the give-way vessel fails to take appropriate action to avoid a collision?
choice_a: The stand-on vessel has no legal ability to take evasive action under any circumstance
choice_b: The stand-on vessel may take whatever action is necessary to avoid collision, including altering course or speed, once it becomes apparent the give-way vessel is not acting properly
choice_c: The stand-on vessel must maintain course and speed no matter what, even into a collision
choice_d: The stand-on vessel should immediately shut off its engine and lights
explanation: While the stand-on vessel should generally maintain course and speed, the Navigation Rules allow it to take independent action to avoid a collision once it is clear the give-way vessel is not responding appropriately.
source_note: Universal Navigation Rules (Inland Rule 17), NASBLA-aligned boating safety curriculum

question: How do the Navigation Rules generally treat a personal watercraft compared to other power-driven vessels?
choice_a: PWCs always have automatic right-of-way over larger vessels
choice_b: PWCs follow a completely separate rulebook unrelated to other vessels
choice_c: A PWC is legally a power-driven vessel and must follow the same right-of-way rules as any other motorboat
choice_d: PWCs are exempt from all Navigation Rules
explanation: A personal watercraft is legally classified as a power-driven vessel, meaning standard meeting, crossing, and overtaking right-of-way rules apply to it the same as they do to any other motorboat.
source_note: Universal Navigation Rules applied to PWC classification (NRS 488.035), NASBLA-aligned boating safety curriculum

question: What does restricted visibility (such as fog, haze, or a desert dust storm) require of vessel operators under the Navigation Rules?
choice_a: Operators may continue at full speed as long as radar is not installed
choice_b: Right-of-way rules remain exactly the same in restricted visibility as in clear weather
choice_c: All vessels must stop moving entirely until visibility fully clears
choice_d: Proceed at a safe speed for the conditions, post a proper lookout, and sound the appropriate fog signals, since normal right-of-way rules cannot be applied when vessels cannot see each other
explanation: In restricted visibility, ordinary crossing/meeting right-of-way rules do not apply because vessels may not be able to see each other visually; operators must slow to a safe speed, keep a proper lookout, and use sound signals, a rule with real relevance near Lake Mead's occasional dust storms.
source_note: Universal Navigation Rules (Inland Rule 19) applied to desert dust-storm visibility conditions near Lake Mead
